q: Dependency vs constituency parsing?
short: Constituency builds nested phrases (NP, VP); dependency links words directly by head → dependent relations with labels. Dependencies handle free word order more naturally and give direct predicate–argument structure.

q: What conditions make a dependency graph a valid tree?
short: Connected (all words reach ROOT), acyclic, single head for every word except ROOT; often also projective (no crossing arcs).
detail: Non-projective trees are allowed in many schemes.

q: What is Universal Dependencies?
short: A project providing consistent POS tags and dependency relations (nsubj, obj, iobj, amod, det, case, obl…) across 100+ languages, so parsers and treebanks are comparable cross-lingually.

q: Describe the arc-eager transitions.
short: SH pushes the buffer front; LA adds buffer front → stack top and pops; RA adds stack top → buffer front and pushes it; RE pops a stack word that already has its head.
detail: Starts with [ROOT], ends when the buffer is empty.
mistakes: Confusing which word becomes the head.

q: How is a transition parser's oracle trained?
short: Convert treebank trees into gold action sequences; extract features of each configuration (words/POS of stack top and buffer front, existing arcs); train a classifier (perceptron, SVM, neural net) to predict the action.
detail: Static oracle; dynamic oracles handle errors.
mistakes: Training on parser outputs instead of gold.

q: What does graph-based parsing optimise?
short: The total score of a spanning tree over all possible head → dependent arcs: G' = argmax Σ w_ij, found exactly with the Chu-Liu-Edmonds MST algorithm.

q: Transition-based vs graph-based: trade-offs?
short: Transition-based: linear time, rich history features, but greedy with error cascades and (basic) projective only. Graph-based: exact global search, non-projective, but arc-factored scores and higher cost (O(n²)–O(n³)).
mistakes: Claiming one dominates in all respects.

q: What are UAS and LAS?
short: Unlabelled attachment score: % of words with the correct head. Labelled attachment score: % with correct head and label. LAS ≤ UAS.
example: One wrong label lowers only LAS.

q: Trace arc-eager on 'He sent her a letter .'.
short: SH; LA sent→He; RA ROOT→sent; RA sent→her; RE; SH a; LA letter→a; RA sent→letter; RE; RA sent→. (10 actions).
detail: Each word shifted/reduced at most once.
example: Labels SBJ, IOBJ, DET, DOBJ, PUNC.
mistakes: Using RA for 'a' (its head is to the right).

q: Apply the perceptron update for SH [5,5,5], LA [5.5,5.5,5.5], active feature 2, predicted LA, gold SH.
short: w_SH += f → [5, 6, 5] (score 6.0); w_LA −= f → [5.5, 4.5, 5.5] (score 4.5); now SH is chosen.

q: Run Chu-Liu-Edmonds on 'John saw Mary'.
short: Greedy heads: John ← saw (30), saw ← John (20), Mary ← saw (30) → cycle {John, saw}, score 50. Rescore into C: root via saw 10 − 20 + 50 = 40; via John 9 − 30 + 50 = 29; Mary via John 11 − 30 + 50 = 31. Pick root→saw, break John→saw: root→saw, saw→John, saw→Mary = 70.
mistakes: Forgetting to add the cycle score.

q: Why do transition parsers suffer error propagation?
short: Each action is chosen greedily and irrevocably from local features; a wrong early arc changes later configurations, which differ from anything seen in gold training, causing further errors.

q: What is non-projectivity and how do parsers handle it?
short: Crossing arcs (discontinuous subtrees), common in free-word-order languages and some English constructions. Graph-based MST handles it directly; transition parsers need extra actions (swap) or pseudo-projective transformations.
example: 'A hearing is scheduled on the issue today'.

q: What features help score arcs in graph-based parsing?
short: Head and dependent words and POS, POS of surrounding and in-between words, arc direction and distance, combinations; in neural parsers, biaffine scores over contextual vectors replace manual features.
detail: Arc-factored: score depends on one arc.
mistakes: Using features of the whole tree in an arc-factored model.

q: Local vs global perceptron training?
short: Transition parsers update after each wrong action (local); graph-based parsers decode the whole tree and update w += f(G_true) − f(G') (global), learning to trade off arcs jointly.

q: Build a relation-extraction system using dependency parses.
short: Parse sentences (UD parser), find entity pairs, extract the shortest dependency path between them (e.g. nsubj ← founded → obj), learn or hand-write patterns over paths, filter with entity types, and output triples for a knowledge graph; evaluate precision on a sample.
detail: Paths are more robust than surface patterns.

q: Why does Chu-Liu-Edmonds' rescoring formula work?
short: Choosing an external arc u → v into a cycle means v loses its internal head arc; the new tree's score equals the cycle's internal score minus that arc plus the new one, so w(u → C) = w(u → v) − w(head(v) → v) + s(C) compares alternatives fairly.
detail: Any MST keeps all but one cycle arc.
follow: Prove the 'all but one arc' claim.
mistakes: Dropping s(C), which is constant but conventional.

q: How do modern neural dependency parsers work?
short: Encode tokens with a BiLSTM or Transformer; for graph-based, score every head–dependent pair with a biaffine function and decode the MST; for transition-based, a feed-forward or neural classifier predicts actions from encoded stack/buffer items. LAS above 90% on many UD treebanks.

q: Parse a language with free word order and a small treebank.
short: Use UD annotation, a graph-based (non-projective) parser on top of a multilingual pre-trained encoder, cross-lingual transfer from related languages, morphological features (case markers), and evaluate LAS on held-out data; consider annotation projection from parallel text.

q: How can the same sentence's constituency and dependency trees be related?
short: Using head-percolation rules, each phrase selects a head child; the head word of each non-head child becomes a dependent of the phrase's head word. Going back is ambiguous (dependencies don't specify all phrase boundaries).
